2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: Single-wave cross-sectional qualitative fieldwork conducted between June and August 2012 with no longitudinal follow-up; interview refusal or non-response rates are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled qualitative case study): No counterfactual or analytical separation between the nascent Bonsucro certification process (pre-audits in eight mills in 2010, internal auditor training in 2011, zero pre-audits among Procana small suppliers, and pending appeals over water limits) and pre-existing drivers of land/water concentration, including 140 years of plantation monoculture, Colombian biofuel blend mandates, CVC regulatory capture, armed conflict, and El Nino droughts.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate documentary specification, weak field compliance verification: Accurately identifies and critiques specific provisions of Bonsucro Version 3.0 (Principle 1 on national tenure law and ILO Convention 169 Articles 13-19; Principle 5 water-use thresholds of 20 kg water/kg sugar, 30 kg/kg ethanol, <130 kg/kg cane, and N/P fertilizer input metrics), EU RED (2009), Colombian Decree #4892 (2012), Law 99 (1993), and local potable-water rules (Decree 1541/78 and Agreement 042/2010), but relies on stakeholder perceptions rather than primary audit or administrative enforcement records and explicitly notes that verifying legal land use was beyond the study's scope.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: Primary data come from unstandardized exploratory interviews without reported interview guides, recording/transcription procedures, or translation protocols, paired with secondary regional statistics; household water-access impacts rely on unverified stakeholder accounts.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak primary measurement (secondary statistics plus qualitative accounts): No original hydrological or household survey measurements were collected; basin-level water allocation and pollution metrics (64% surface water and 88% groundwater concessions held by sugar producers; 76% of N/P/pesticide load) are cited secondarily from Perez et al. (2011) and CVC reports, while community dry-season water shortages and forced household water purchases are documented only via qualitative interview summaries.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: Although the paper juxtaposes industry association perspectives (Asocana, Procana) with critical agricultural researcher, small farmer, and rural resident accounts, the absence of a qualitative coding protocol or participant-by-category breakdown prevents verification against selective quotation.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: Relies on purposive selection of 14 exploratory interviewees across seven broad stakeholder groups in Valle del Cauca (plus an unspecified number of displaced rural community residents mentioned on p. 465) without reporting the sampling frame, recruitment mechanics, sample distribution across groups, or refusal rates.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Selfa, Bain, and Moreno (2014) present a primary qualitative case study examining how Colombia's political economy of land and water governance shapes the implementation and limits of Bonsucro sustainability certification in the Valle del Cauca sugarcane-ethanol sector. Because all quantitative figures in the paper (e.g., land Gini/ownership shares, CVC surface and groundwater concession shares, river nutrient loads) are cited from secondary sources rather than original quantitative data collection or analysis, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the appropriate appraisal instrument. Methodological strengths include clearly articulated theoretical aims grounded in Ribot and Peluso's theory of access (Q1-Q3), detailed documentary scrutiny of Bonsucro Version 3.0 Principles 1 and 5 alongside national and regional water regulations (Decree 1541/78, Agreement 042/2010, Law 99 of 1993), and balanced presentation of contrasting narratives from industry associations (Asocana, Procana), critics, and rural residents (Q9-Q10). However, methodological reporting is sparse across core empirical procedures: recruitment mechanics and group-level sample counts for the 14 exploratory interviews (and their relation to rural community residents cited on p. 465) are unspecified (Q4: Can't tell); interview protocols, recording/transcription, and translation procedures are omitted (Q5: Can't tell); researcher reflexivity is absent (Q6: No); formal ethics/consent procedures are unreported despite sensitive conflict/corruption topics (Q7: Can't tell); and qualitative coding/analytic methods are not described (Q8: Can't tell). Moreover, because Bonsucro certification in Colombia was still in pre-audit and standard-negotiation stages in 2012, conclusions about certification reinforcing water and land grabs are partly prospective and cannot isolate Bonsucro's effect from long-standing state policies and CVC governance.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (4 Can't tell items and 1 No item out of Q1-Q9)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative case study (in-depth exploratory stakeholder interviews paired with documentary analysis of certification standards, laws, and secondary regional reports)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methods description in a single paragraph at the end of 'Biofuels, land and water grabs: prospects for governance' (PDF p. 4, p. 458), supplemented by brief mention of rural resident interviews in 'Water grabs and Bonsucro certification' (PDF p. 11, p. 465), scope limitation in Footnote 6 (PDF p. 8, p. 462), regulatory/standard analysis across PDF pp. 7-11 (pp. 461-465), and Acknowledgments/author bios (PDF pp. 13-14, pp. 467-468).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component consists of in-depth exploratory qualitative interviews with 14 sugarcane/ethanol stakeholders (plus rural residents) in Valle del Cauca between June and August 2012, paired with qualitative documentary critique of Bonsucro standards and Colombian policies. All quantitative statistics on land concentration and water concessions/pollution are cited from secondary literature (e.g., Perez et al. 2011; Marin et al. 2011; CVC 2011; DANE 2012) rather than a primary quantitative empirical component, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the exact matching tool rather than MMAT, JBI, or ROBINS-I.
